item.title: Chromosome 14: The Myth of a Single Gene for Hoarding
item.description:
Hoarding

Chromosome 14: The Myth of a Single Gene for Hoarding

From chromosome 14 to polygenics, scientists rethink the genetics of hoarding.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Initially, chromosome 14 was implicated as a locus of hoarding.
  • As more studies were performed, this concept became untenable.
  • Now, we know that there is no single chromosome that can be implicated in the development of hoarding.
  • Rather, the underlying origin is polygenic, essentially an underlying architecture throughout the brain.
A slide section similar to ones I studied as a student.: Condensed chromosome (purple rod) inside a bone marrow undergoing division
Source: Makysm, CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

Many years ago, I studied the components of a cell, including its nuclear material. This experience and my recent essay, “Is Hoarding in Our Genes? What a Landmark Twin Study Reveals,” led me to investigate the potential contribution of a chromosomal component to the known genetics of hoarding. What I found is fascinating and worth examining as part of the unfolding story of the origins of hoarding,

The Initial Research

Hoarding disorder is often described as if it might be “caused” by a single errant chromosome, but the trajectory of genetic research, from early linkage studies to contemporary twin and genome‑wide studies, points instead to a complex genetic architecture that resists reductionism. The story that begins with chromosome 14 ends, at least for now, with a polygenic finale, one distributed across the genome and filtered through cognition, affect, and experience.

The 2009 OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder) Collaborative Genetics Study is a natural starting point because it crystallized early enthusiasm for a specific locus for compulsive hoarding. The authors reported suggestive linkage to a region on chromosome 14, with stronger signals in families that had multiple relatives who hoard, and additional linkage findings on other chromosomes in different family subsets. Their language was cautious, emphasizing linkage rather than causation, but the notion that hoarding might “live” on chromosome 14 echoed quickly through the clinical and popular literature.

A Deeper Dive

As more studies accumulated, however, that narrative became harder to sustain. Family and twin research consistently shows that hoarding symptoms are more common among first‑degree relatives of people with a hoarding disorder, and that hoarding traits are moderately to highly heritable. However, twin modeling does not point to a single locus; instead, it separates shared and non‑shared environmental influences and shows substantial but imperfect genetic overlap across hoarding dimensions, such as excessive acquisition and difficulty discarding. This pattern is what one would expect from a distributed genetic architecture: multiple genetic influences of varying effect that cluster around related traits but do not collapse neatly into a single chromosomal “cause.”

The more recent era of genome‑wide association studies reinforced this picture. A large meta‑analysis of hoarding symptoms in over 27,000 individuals demonstrated that hoarding is prevalent and heritable, with genetic factors explaining a significant portion of variance. Yet no single variant achieved genome‑wide significance. The signals that did emerge were small, scattered across several chromosomal regions, and best interpreted as pieces of a broader polygenic landscape. Importantly, these findings remained after controlling for obsessive‑compulsive symptoms, underscoring that hoarding’s genetic risk is not merely a reflection of OCD’s genetic profile.

In parallel, narrative and systematic reviews of hoarding etiology have concluded that while genetic contributions are clear, specific chromosomal findings, including the much‑cited chromosome 14 linkage, are inconsistent and preliminary, and must be understood in the context of cognitive, emotional, and environmental mechanisms that shape the clinical phenotype.

Summary

From a clinical and conceptual perspective, it is more accurate to speak of “genetic architecture underlying hoarding” than of direct chromosome causes. Chromosome 14 still deserves mention, but only as an early signal on a broader map of susceptibility. Framing hoarding in terms of genetic architecture keeps our focus on distributed vulnerability, developmental pathways, and modifiable mechanisms, rather than a deterministic single-chromosome story that current evidence does not support.

item.title: Do You Feel Dignity in Your Relationship?
item.description:
Relationships

Do You Feel Dignity in Your Relationship?

How protecting psychological needs makes relationship communication respectful.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Communication falters when people feel dismissed, controlled, shamed, or unsafe.
  • Violations of dignity can spark defensiveness, withdrawal, rage, or retaliation.
  • Respectful communication protects dignity while still naming harmful behavior.

Imagine a partner who responds to every expression of hurt with the same three words: “You’re too sensitive.”

At first, this sounds like a disagreement about interpretation—one person feels injured, the other finds the reaction exaggerated. But the deeper problem may not be the sentence; maybe it is the pattern. Emotional reality is minimized. Autonomy is narrowed because one person is told how they are allowed to feel. Competence is questioned because their perception is framed as irrational. And dignity is injured because vulnerability is met with dismissal. Over time, the question shifts.

From: “What happened between us?”
To: “Am I even allowed to feel what I feel?”

Communication is never only an exchange of words. It is also an exchange of psychological signals. Every conversation tells us something about whether we are safe, respected, included, taken seriously, and allowed to remain ourselves.

From the perspective of the theory of universal psychological needs (Sefik Tagay, 2025), human experience and behavior are organized around six basic needs: safety and predictability, attachment and belonging, autonomy and influence, competence and efficacy, dignity and recognition, and meaning and coherence. In conversation, these needs are touched in the smallest moments—a tone of voice, an interruption, a correction, a silence, a joke, or a boundary.

Among them, dignity has a special role. People can often tolerate disagreement, and sometimes even criticism. But they rarely stay open when they feel humiliated.

Dignity is not only a psychological idea. In Germany, it opens the Basic Law: “Human dignity shall be inviolable.” The U.S. Constitution contains no equivalent opening clause, yet dignity appears as a moral thread in constitutional ideas of liberty, equality, due process, and protection from degrading treatment. The contrast points to a psychological truth: Human beings need more than the freedom to speak. They also need forms of speech that do not destroy the personhood of others.

When Dignity Is Wounded

This matters because dignity violations are not neutral. Being dismissed, ridiculed, or treated as beneath respect can threaten the sense of self. For some people, that threat becomes hurt, shame, or withdrawal. For others, especially when self-worth is fragile, inflated, or highly dependent on admiration, it may be externalized as rage.

What begins as humiliation can become anger. What begins as anger can become retaliation. Research on threatened egotism helps explain why. People high in narcissistic traits are not simply too confident; they can be unusually reactive when their self-image is challenged, and narcissism is linked to aggression, especially under provocation. Vulnerable narcissism, in particular, has been tied to rage, hostility, angry rumination, and reactive aggression. In intimate relationships, narcissism has also shown a small but significant association with partner violence perpetration, especially psychological and cyber forms.

In close relationships, this becomes especially destructive. A partner who experiences criticism as humiliation may respond with a counterattack; reflection is needed. The goal shifts from understanding to restoring superiority—mocking, blaming, punishing, withdrawing affection, making the other person “pay.” Anger can harden into vindictive hostility.

A needs-based approach does not diagnose the other person. But it helps us see the danger of repeated violations of dignity, which can turn a dialogue into a struggle over worth, control, and self-protection.

None of this means conflict should be softened. Some behavior must be challenged. Some boundaries must be set. Some statements are harmful and need to be named. Respect is not agreement. Tolerance is not passivity. A respectful conversation can be firm, critical, and morally clear. What makes it respectful is that it criticizes behavior without destroying personhood.

That distinction matters most in harmful patterns. If one partner repeatedly dismisses feelings, mocks vulnerability, or turns every criticism back on the other, the task is not simply to “communicate better.” It is to recognize the pattern. Needs-sensitive communication is not submission; it does not ask people to endure contempt more politely.

A clear boundary might sound like this: “I’m willing to talk about what happened, but I’m not willing to have my feelings dismissed or mocked. If we continue, we need to speak in a way that protects both of our dignity.”

The sentence keeps dialogue open, names the problem, and protects dignity without attacking the other’s worth.

The opposite of dignified dialogue is not disagreement. It is contempt—which reduces a person to a flaw, a failure, or a category, and communicates: You are beneath respect. Once contempt enters, people stop listening and start defending. Dignified dialogue allows conflict without humiliation, criticism without devaluation, and boundaries without dehumanization.

Five Rules for Dignified Dialogue

1. Protect dignity before making your point.
Ask: Can I say this without humiliating the other person?

2. Focus on behavior, not personhood.
Name what was harmful, unfair, or painful, without turning one action into a verdict on the whole person.

3. Use boundaries instead of contempt.
A boundary says, “This is what I can or cannot continue.” Contempt says, “You are beneath respect.”

4. Name feelings without weaponizing them.
“I felt hurt when that happened” opens a door. “You always destroy everything” closes it.

5. Leave when dignity cannot be protected.
If a conversation repeatedly becomes mocking, threatening, or emotionally unsafe, ending it may be the most respectful act toward oneself.

Good communication does not eliminate conflict; it makes conflict more humane. When dignity is protected, people no longer spend all their energy on defense. They can listen, disagree, repair, and sometimes change. In that sense, dignified dialogue is more than a skill. It is a form of psychological care

item.title: Acceleration and Alienation
item.description:
Productivity

Acceleration and Alienation

Why connection is the key to thriving in a world that won’t slow down.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Time-saving technologies can still leave us feeling time-poor.
  • Social acceleration can fuel feelings of alienation.
  • Slowing down often isn’t enough to overcome burnout.
  • Meaningful connection helps us thrive in an age of acceleration.
Source: Getty Images / Unsplash

We are living through an age of rapid technological transformation. Each development promises to maximize efficiency and enhance productivity. And yet, the reality is that most of us feel more time-pressed than ever before. We feel like we are constantly struggling to keep up. We are working harder and moving faster, and yet things don’t feel like they’re getting much better.

For centuries, new technologies have been developed to help us do more, in less time, with less effort. Whether that goes back to the invention of the washing machine, which saved the hours it took to go and wash your clothes in a well or stream, or more recent advancements brought by AI that can answer all your emails in seconds, new technologies have, in many ways, made life easier. So, why does it still feel as though we’re always rushing and running out of time?

Part of the answer lies in the human tendency for acclimatization. Our minds quickly adjust to changes in our environment, and with them, our expectations shift. Whilst previously you might have been expected to send a few letters each week, now you are expected to respond to hundreds of messages and emails, to be on call all hours of the day. The technologies that promised freedom and ease simply raise expectations, setting a new baseline to keep up with.

But it isn’t just about shifting expectations. Indeed, the paradox of time-saving innovation is explained by sociologist Hartmut Rosa’s theory of social acceleration, which describes how technological developments not only change what we do but also how we experience and perceive time itself. Modernization, he suggests, is best understood as a process of speeding up the world.

Ultimately, acceleration is a defining feature of modern society. Our institutions and economies depend on continual growth and innovation. We have to keep producing, improving, and optimizing simply to maintain the status quo. In this way, modern life can feel like running on a treadmill. The pace keeps increasing, and we struggle to keep up, only to realize that we’ve been running on the spot.

At a planetary level, we know that continued growth in a closed system is unsustainable. But what is less often discussed is why this is also—at a human level—impossible. People cannot be expected to continually produce more at a faster pace without also burning out.

Here, Rosa explains that the psychological cost of acceleration is alienation. When our attention is focused on maximizing efficiency and productivity, we lose the ability to really connect with the things we are doing in a way that gives them meaning.

We can see the effects of this in rising levels of stress and anxiety. These are not simply individual afflictions, but symptoms of a culture that demands that we move faster and, in doing so, pulls us away from mindful connection.

Now, the obvious solution is to slow down. And in some ways, that can be incredibly helpful. Taking time to rest, to distance yourself from the need to constantly optimize. However, in and of itself, this will not fix the problem. Instead, Rosa argues that we should focus on resonance, rebuilding meaningful connections with people, ideas, nature, and the activities that matter to us.

Importantly, resonance is not just about doing things more slowly, but more intentionally. The goal is not to reject technology, efficiency, or modern life, but to pay more attention to how we relate to the things we do.

Instead of squeezing in a gym session before work, make time to get outside and move your body, noticing the feeling of the fresh air moving through your lungs. Rather than spending hours messaging your friends back and forth, use that time to have a meaningful conversation—whether that’s connecting with somebody close to you or chatting to the person who works at your local shop.

This shift can be revolutionary because we find energy in connection. While acceleration and alienation make us feel depleted and drained, resonance is invigorating. Let’s take an example. Say you get home from a stressful day rushing through your to-do list at work. To save time and unwind, you pop a ready meal in the microwave and scroll on your phone with the TV in the background. You’ve fed and entertained yourself, but neither has replenished you.

Imagine instead that you cook dinner, finding yourself engrossed in the process of preparing your food. You go to the cinema, giving the film your full attention and allowing yourself to be moved by the story. The same functions are fulfilled, but the second leaves you feeling revitalized.

Ultimately, to thrive in a world that shows no sign of slowing down, it’s important that we build resonance into our lives. As individuals, that means connecting with the people, places, and activities that give our lives meaning. As a society, that means creating and investing in spaces that make connection possible.

item.title: Why We Should Protect Childlike Imagination
item.description:
Imagination

Why We Should Protect Childlike Imagination

We train creativity out of kids, then pay to get it back. Here's how to keep it.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • The best creative breakthroughs come from play and a little pressure, not shortcutting straight to the answer.
  • We abandon childlike imagination partly out of ego, and now can hide our unfinished thinking behind AI polish.
  • Businesses now pay to reintroduce the childlike thinking we've trained ourselves out of.
  • The way back isn't a new app; it's a pencil, paper, and permission to make a mess.
Source: Cartoon by author Lisa Rothstein

In my years in advertising, those of us in the so-called Creative Department of the agency often worried we’d had our last good idea. But eventually, we always proved ourselves wrong. Our imaginations and our conversations with each other would create a flurry of improbable connections and laugh-out-loud silly notions, yielding something magical out of nothing.

The magic came from the play, and yes, a little from the pressure too. Both forced us somewhere we couldn’t have gotten on our own.

Today we’ve short-circuited both, defaulting to the easy solution: offloading the thinking onto technology, fast-forwarding past the childlike part that produces the unexpected answer. We've forgotten how to think like a child—open to every possibility, endlessly inventive, not looking for shortcuts, but always seeking magic.

There’s another reason we’ve abandoned our playful nature, and it’s less flattering: ego. We want to look smart. We don’t want to look silly, unfinished, or like we might fail in front of other people. AI is the perfect accomplice because it hands us something polished and professional to hide behind.

But the rough, the imperfect, the visibly-still-thinking is exactly where the magic lives. A child doesn’t care if the drawing is good. That’s their superpower. We trade it away the moment we start caring what the room thinks.

I learned this early. One of my very first clients was Kentucky Fried Chicken, and they needed a newspaper campaign that would get people buying their chicken for more occasions. We had a lot of really lame and corny ideas.

Then, almost out of boredom, I picked up a black grease pencil and started drawing right on top of the photos of the packaging. I gave the box wheels, and suddenly we were taking KFC on a road trip. I scribbled a TV antenna on it (back in the day when people still remembered TVs with antennas!), and now it was dinner in front of the game. Within an hour, we had a dozen scenes—picnics, class reunions, study sessions, moving parties—each one sparked by a crude mark on a picture, each one letting the reader’s own imagination supply the rest.

A KFC campaign I worked on. The grease-pencil "doodle" became the finished ad.
Source: KFC national advertising co-op, 1984

And here’s the part I still love: those ugly grease-pencil scribbles didn’t just spark the campaign. They became it. The ads ran exactly like that: wheels, antenna, and all. No one cared that the drawings were rough. That was the whole point.

I recently discovered a company built entirely on injecting that childlike thinking back into real business situations. It’s called ConsultingKids, the brainchild of a Dutch entrepreneur named Bas Warmerdam. He organizes think tanks of fifth-graders to help companies solve real problems—translating the business case into games and language kids understand, letting them problem-solve in their own idea-flooded way, then translating their solutions back into business terms.

He also runs a workshop that reintroduces grown-ups to the imagination they still have but have forgotten how to reach. There’s a quiet irony in it: as Sir Ken Robinson famously argued, we spend our early years training the creativity out of children—and then, decades later, pay consultants to put it back.

If I had to name one path back to your childlike imagination, it wouldn’t be a new app. It would be the oldest tools we have: a pencil, a piece of paper, and permission to make a mess. Doodle your way toward the idea instead of prompting your way to it. You’ll see connections you’d never have found otherwise—not because the drawing is good, but because you stopped caring whether it was.

That’s the part of you that once conjured a friend out of thin air. It’s still in there. Go let it play.

item.title: Why Your Body Freezes, Flees, or Fights Under Stress
item.description:
Stress

Why Your Body Freezes, Flees, or Fights Under Stress

Understanding how your nervous system drives your fear response.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Fear activates hormones like adrenaline and cortisol, priming the body for survival.
  • Fight, flight, and freeze reflect escalating threat responses in the nervous system.
  • The sympathetic system drives escape, while the parasympathetic system can shut the body down.
  • Physical symptoms—from tension to dizziness—are normal outputs of these survival systems.

How Anxiety Manifests in the Body: Fight, Flight, Freeze

Similar to stress, when we feel fearful, the amygdala activates the HPA axis, releasing cortisol, epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine, and acetylcholine. These hormones stimulate our nervous systems immediately, but their effects can be felt for up to an hour once they’re released. Depending on the extent of the fear, the release of these hormones can activate one of several fear responses: fight, flight, or freeze. A flight response activates under greater levels of fear than the fight response, and the freeze response activates under even greater levels as a last resort against danger.

For example, when a lizard relaxing on a warm rock catches sight of an encroaching snake, it will prepare to defend itself (fight), run away if it can’t adequately defend itself (flight), or go limp to feign death if it can’t escape (freeze). Each of these three responses is associated with a different branch of the nervous system.

Explaining the Fight, Flight, and Freeze Responses

The fight response is associated with the somatic nervous system. The somatic nervous system allows us to use our voluntary muscles, like our hands and feet, to fight in defense against potential threats.

The flight response is associated with the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system.1,2 The sympathetic nervous system activates involuntary striated muscles, including our heart, and stimulates our brain, preparing us to flee from danger. Activation of the sympathetic nervous system releases epinephrine (adrenaline) into the bloodstream and norepinephrine into the brain. When the sympathetic nervous system becomes highly activated in response to fear, it can lead to shaking, shortness of breath, and hyperventilation.

The freeze response is associated with the parasympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system.1,2 The parasympathetic nervous system deactivates involuntary smooth muscles like our heart and deactivates parts of our central nervous system, freezing us in place. When the parasympathetic nervous system becomes highly activated in response to fear, it can lead to gastrointestinal and cognitive perceptual disturbances, including irritable bowel, nausea, and migraines.

Just like the lizard in the previous example, we all experience these responses as our nervous system activates.

What Does Fight, Flight, or Freeze Actually Look Like?

When the body enters a fight response, physical tension manifests as clenched fingers, a tight jaw, and strained muscles in the neck, stomach, or shoulders—often leading to headaches, sighing, or chronic issues like fibromyalgia. This state is also characterized by dilated pupils as the body braces for confrontation. If the reaction shifts toward flight, the system gears up for escape: heart rate and blood pressure climb, breathing becomes shallow or rapid, and “butterflies” flutter in the stomach alongside twitchy limbs. One might experience a dry mouth, cold shivering, or sweating, while the digestive system slows, causing urinary retention or constipation.

In contrast, the freeze response can cause the heart to skip a beat and the pupils to constrict, often leading to a sense of immobilization or “jelly legs.” This state frequently impacts the gut and lungs, resulting in nausea, excessive belching, diarrhea, or even asthma attacks due to airway constriction. Neurologically and sensorially, a person might endure dizziness, blurred vision, ringing in the ears, or migraines caused by dilating blood vessels. Finally, the mental strain of freezing can result in “foggy thinking,” memory loss, crying, or, in extreme cases, hallucinations as the mind struggles to process the perceived threat.

This post is an excerpt from my ebook, How to Live a Stress-Free Life: 10 Proven Ways to Reduce Anxiety and Calm Your Mind.

item.title: Is Your Identity Keeping You From Making Positive Changes?
item.description:
Identity

Is Your Identity Keeping You From Making Positive Changes?

We think of personal change as something difficult, but it can happen quickly.

Posted July 1, 2026

Making a pivotal life change—such as overcoming a toxic behavior or setting boundaries with a difficult individual—can often seem impossible. Often, though, entrenched beliefs about our identity and who we think we are can get in the way of making positive change.

I witnessed firsthand how difficult making changes was while working as a therapist at an intensive outpatient eating disorder clinic. One of the patients, Amber (not her real name), was a 32-year-old with a long history of bulimia and alcohol. No matter what we tried, Amber could not break free of her eating disorder behavior.

Looking back, I’ve come to understand that Amber’s sense of identity had become strongly fused with her eating disorder. She more than once said to me, “Who would I be without it?” To truly change and heal, Amber would need to move beyond her lifelong identity and set new, healthy boundaries.

Interestingly, I’ve since repeatedly heard the refrain “Who would I be without my (anxiety, depression, etc., fill in the blank)?” Sometimes it’s subtle, other times explicit. Either way, when anyone expresses a need for change, they may fear tearing down what is a well-crafted, lifelong identity.

This is why I often call the identity—the ‘I’ ‘me’ ‘my’ and ‘mine’—the Wizard of I, the hidden part of us that is constructing the identity, as well as protecting and defending it! This hidden self fragments the wholeness of our present moment experiences into little pieces of good, bad, right, and wrong. Protecting this identity is often what makes us get defensive and angry. We may not even know that our Wizard of I is constantly monitoring and getting in the way of our direct experience and our joy.

So how can we stealthily change and get around that silent partner—our identity, whose job it is to maintain its place of supremacy in our lives? I know that sounds like one of those “how do you change a lightbulb” jokes, but it’s worth considering, and may not be as daunting as it sounds.

Present Moment Awareness Brings Stealthy Change

Not many people mention it, but mindfulness and present moment awareness are integrative practices. Present moment awareness brings us into our entire being, mind and body. That means it can help us know when we’re getting too stressed, out of the body, or stuck in unproductive thought caused by The Wizard of I.

This is why the experience of being present in the here and now is so important for living a more balanced life, and why it's being applied in various therapy modalities. Research has even shown that present moment awareness helps combat vets with PTSD move their awareness away from rumination and back to the present moment, where they can recognize that they’re safe and respond to what’s happening right around them.

Learning to get in the present moment strengthens the prefrontal cortex, or what I call the Reflect and Relate Module of the brain.

Practicing presence stealthily rebuilds the pause, think, and respond circuitry of the brain, as opposed to the react and repeat circuitry of the stress system.

Here are two easy-to-use practices for getting past the identity and responding freshly, with present moment awareness.

  1. Savor an In-Between Moment. The practice of noticing the in-between helps you pause, come back to the moment, and steep yourself in the here and now. Anytime you are standing in line or just waiting in your car at a stoplight, notice one new thing in your surroundings. This could be a color, a shape, an object, or even the sound of your own breath. You can also journal these “little, ordinary moments” to start. Make sure to share those little moments with others. In this way, you're not only reflecting, but relating these little moments. By both reflecting and relating, the brain more strongly encodes these memories. These are the precious moments that make up a life well lived!
  2. Find One Pleasant Thing in the Here and Now. The practice of noting pleasantness can help shift anyone out of negativity and toward joy. Can you find one pleasant thing around you right now? This can be a favorite color, a sound, a pleasant flower or a work of art you like. It could be something that makes you smile or laugh. Also, each time you move into a new room or space, find one more pleasant thing. This stealthy repetition rewires the brain, gets you out of your head, and propels you into the here and now moment.

Conclusion

These are just a couple of stealth methods for creating change by getting past old belief systems or identities. My book Simply Mindful Resilience features over 100 different methods for embracing present moment awareness, overcoming obstacles and building positive change.

Remember, the present moment doesn't define you or try to hold you to a set of beliefs like an identity does.

The present moment is free. It costs you nothing. And it comes unencumbered from the chains of expectations, beliefs, judgments and rules that an identity forces you to abide by.

And, once you practice being in the present moment, you may discover that you are not who you think you are. Most importantly, you may find that making those new, positive changes is easier, too.

item.title: Jaret Reddick and the Power of “Almost”
item.description:
Depression

Jaret Reddick and the Power of “Almost”

The Bowling For Soup front man discusses the role of communication in managing health.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Physical and mental health issues may cause suffering and interfere with life functioning.
  • Bowling for Soup founding member Jaret Reddick has struggled with both.
  • Reddick emphasizes communication as a key aspect of coping with physical and mental health issues.

Bowling for Soup is considered by many to be one of the best pop punk bands of all time. Their 2004 hit song “Almost” is an upbeat, playful homage to unfulfilled teenage dreams. Over the past 20 years, singer-songwriter and founding band member Jaret Reddick has become a prominent mental health advocate, sharing his struggle with both ulcerative colitis and depression. Reddick founded the non-profit organization Punk Rock Saves Lives and recently appeared in the movie Heavy Healing, which focuses on how music helps people cope with health issues. And in talking to Reddick, I began to hear the song "Almost" as a tribute to people who struggle to achieve their life goals as they cope with their health issues.

Jaret Reddick
Source: Amy Barry/Used With Permission

Reddick shared his evolution of the meaning of "Almost." "We all have these … big aspirations ... but we lose our footing along the way," Reddick told me. "I feel like that song … sort of deepened for me over time … these dreams that we sort of never get to."

Reddick described how his ulcerative colitis would disrupt his life, including interfering with his participation as a contestant on the game show The Floor. "I was on tour ... I had an ulcerative colitis flare-up that was getting to be unmanageable. I was barely making it on stage and off stage without a major issue happening," he recalled. "I had to do the unthinkable and pull out of that thing two days before I left … I didn't leave the house for two months."

While his ulcerative colitis often interfered with his work and personal life, Reddick described how his strong sense of purpose helped him stay focused on his goals. "You've got to figure this out … you have to be able to do things. You have to be able to go out to eat with your family ... go to the movies," Reddick explained. "Me canceling a show … It affects the fans … my crew … It affects people financially ... emotionally … It's a lot of reasons why I have to hold it together."

One of the reasons why Reddick was able to effectively cope with ulcerative colitis was that he understood his diagnosis, symptoms and treatment plan. In contrast, when he first began experiencing symptoms of depression at the age of 40, he was baffled by his experience. "I was a guy that thought depression meant sad … And that's not me ... I didn’t get the diagnosis for a while," he said. "When I got ulcerative colitis … I could physically tell you all of these things about it. So it made sense to me."

Reddick soon learned that depression represented a different type of challenge because it undermined the motivation he relied upon to cope and work hard to achieve his goals. "That was like being hit by a train," Reddick described. "Depression — I mean, there was just no desire. There was no motivation … It was enough for me to get up, get my kids ready for school, get them out the door, make sure the dog goes outside, and then right back to that bed in the fetal position until I had to be on again."

article continues after advertisement

The lack of clarity made coping with depression difficult. He didn't understand his symptoms and couldn't communicate his experience to others, including his bandmates. "It's a cycle, because the more you can't figure yourself out ... the more you can't motivate yourself ... the worse that it gets," he recalled. "So it's very interesting for me to hear that from my friends' standpoint … 'We had no idea. We just thought you were just moving on … You're just always doing other stuff."

The first step that broke this vicious cycle was Reddick finding a doctor who was able to diagnose his depression and engage in a collaborative relationship. "I had a doctor that would listen, and he was just like … 'Let's try this, let's try this,'" Reddick explained. "There is no magic pill ... I tell people who are first starting to deal with it ... 'Listen, go to your doctor. Trust your doctor. You're going to try two different meds at least, and they're not going to work. And you're going to get frustrated ... Get in there and do the work and tell him, tell him exactly how it makes you feel every single time.'"

His ability to understand his diagnosis and communicate about treatment allowed him to be more honest and forthright with friends and family. "The one thing that I've really learned is communication. Fighting any of it on your own is just not productive … The minute you share it, it's a weight off your shoulders," he described. "And now I can come out of the back of the bus and I can say, 'Hey guys, I'm not feeling great today. I just want you to know if I'm a little off. It's not you. Everything's fine' ... I can tell my wife, 'I'm having a low tide this week. I just want you to know it's not you' ... If I do need a minute ... and if I can't get it, I just f*cking announce it ... 'I gotta have a minute' ... And I just kind of go off somewhere by myself."

article continues after advertisement

Having more clarity around the diagnosis, symptoms and treatment of depression has also allowed Reddick to be respectful of his own mental health journey. "I'm going to be honest that pushing through is still hard," Reddick described. "It's very, very easy to get up and brush your teeth and turn right back around and get back in that bed. It is really, really easy to do."

As a result, he realizes that sometimes, "Almost" is more than enough. "My thing is always try and see the sun today. If you can drink a lot of water, breathe and give yourself grace, man," Reddick said. "If you got out of bed and did ... one thing today, that's more than really anybody should expect from that."

item.title: The Worst Scorecards Are the Ones We Keep in Our Heads
item.description:
Happiness

The Worst Scorecards Are the Ones We Keep in Our Heads

Most of us keep score on a variety of things, and none of it leads to happiness.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Having more does not make people happy.
  • It seems that many people are so busy keeping score that they stop living life.
  • You can learn to shift your scorekeeping to the things that will make you a better a human being.
Source: Andrii Yalanskyi / Adobe Stock

I am an avid golfer. I keep score every time I play a round of golf. Like many serious players, I even submit my scores to the United States Golf Association’s Golf Handicap Information Network (GHIN)—a nationwide score tracking system that maintains my handicap round-to-round. It’s a terrific tool that enables me to measure my progress week to week. But I don’t use it to see how I’m doing compared to my playing partners.

Of course, I used to.

Like many naturally competitive people, I wanted to see if I was playing better than my friends. It’s a quasi-keeping up with the Joneses tendency that I quickly recognized was not a source of inspiration or happiness, so I stopped. Cold turkey. No more comparing myself to my golf buddies. And, guess what? I’m happier, and I’m playing better golf as a result.

Comparison Is a Trap

Think about all the invisible scorecards a typical person might have cluttering their psyche at any point in time:

  • Income
  • Social status
  • Fitness
  • Parenting skills
  • Houses
  • Cars
  • Your toys

You name it, people keep score, and it’s not healthy.

Why?

Because having more or better things does not make you happy. Sure, a nice income can make your life more comfortable. But happier? Nope.

It’s a trap. You think being “better” than your friends and neighbors is somehow going to make you feel more fulfilled and gratified. It doesn’t.

In fact, accumulating “stuff’ often makes life more complicated. Now, you have to protect it—and, most of the time, there are factors that you don’t control that can wreak havoc on what you’ve collected and kept score on.

Outside Factors Often Interfere

Let’s consider some of the things we might keep score on and recognize how little we actually control, like:

  • Your new boss might not like you, and you might lose your job.
  • You might get sick and fall out of shape.
  • Your kids might make poor choices and get into some kind of big trouble.
  • Your house, your car, and your toys might all get lost in a fire.

If we define ourselves by what we have, we just might find ourselves worrying about what we have lost.

It seems we’re so busy keeping score that we stop living life. So, what do we do?

Practical Strategies to Help You Stop Keeping Score

Here are some strategies that you can use to shift your scorekeeping tendencies and discover happiness instead:

1. Redefine what “winning” means.

Recognize that you don’t have to beat someone else to win. A better definition is to do your best and forget the rest. When the process of “winning” is focused internally (instead of externally), we find satisfaction from living our best life and not worrying about being better than someone else.

2. Separate your identity from your “stuff.”

You are not your car, house, kids, or bank account. You are a friend, parent, colleague, and community member. Focus your attention on being really good at being those things, and your fixation on being better than others will fade. You will begin to recognize that the way we make people “feel” is far richer than having more than the next person.

3. Replace comparison with curiosity.

Comparison fuels insecurity; curiosity fuels growth. Instead of being driven to “win,” focus on gaining a better understanding of who you are, what you have learned, and seeking out the things that pleasantly surprise you. If you do that, your life will be charmed.

4. Practice gratitude.

Life is so much better when we stop and smell the roses! Take time every day to appreciate all that you have: your health, your family, your material possessions. Work on being truly grateful, and you will begin to stop worrying about getting more because you will be satisfied with what you have.

5. Be kinder to yourself.

Perfection is not a realistic expectation to put on someone. Why do we put it on ourselves? It’s kinder to give yourself a break when things don’t go the way you planned. Let’s face it, they rarely do. As mentioned above, we have so little control to begin with. So, stop taking it out on yourself when things go south, and you will stop competing so aggressively with your friends.

To close, keeping my golf scores is a wonderful motivator. It’s internally focused, and it helps me identify the things that I need to improve to play better golf and enjoy the sport even more than I do today. I invite you to do the same—shift your scorekeeping to the things that you want to improve in your life to make you a better person and enhance your happiness.

item.title: 2 Habits of Loyal Partners
item.description:
Relationships

2 Habits of Loyal Partners

These two habits take love and turn it into long-term loyalty.

Posted July 1, 2026

Source: Andrik Langfield / Unsplash

Academics describe loyalty as more than just a feeling that two people have about each other. It’s something you should be able to regularly observe in your partner’s daily habits — whether they stay consistent in what they say and do, and whether they protect your dignity when life gets stressful or messy.

The rest is just what that looks like in practice.

1. The Words and Actions of Loyal Partners Consistently Match

We usually notice inconsistency in its extreme forms, like a promise that never gets followed through on, or the repeated “I’ll change” that never quite becomes change. But most of the time, it’s actually even subtler than that: small mismatches that add up until trust feels effortful.

In a seminal study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researchers looked at partner regulation: the subtle (and sometimes not-so-subtle) ways people try to influence or reshape their partner’s behavior over time.

What they found is fairly intuitive. When people engaged in more attempts to regulate their partner, they tended to experience lower ideal-perception consistency — the sense that their partner naturally fits what they value. And that drop in consistency was linked to overall lower relationship quality.

Worse, this led to a vicious cycle. Lower perceived fit tended to increase regulation attempts, which in turn tended to further weaken that sense of fit over time. The more a relationship starts to feel like it requires correction, the more fragile its sense of alignment becomes.

A simple example makes this easier to picture. Imagine your partner repeatedly says they’ll communicate more but keeps defaulting to silence during stress. Or imagine that they’ve promised you emotional presence multiple times, but still check out when things get hard. Each instance on its own might be explainable. But over time, the pattern matters more than the explanation.

At a certain point, words stop reliably predicting what comes next. But that’s exactly what loyalty really buys in a relationship: consistency and predictability. When a partner’s intentions and behavior generally line up, you don’t have to re-evaluate what their promises mean in practice constantly.

2. Loyal Partners Defend Your Dignity

Every relationship eventually runs into stress. There will always be a chance of external pressure, conflict, social friction, or misunderstanding. When it does eventually happen, which it always does, what matters is how you manage it.

Research on dyadic coping (how couples deal with stress together) gives a useful framework here. In a 2019 systematic review published in Frontiers in Psychology, researchers identified different ways partners respond to stress, ranging from supportive and collaborative responses to withdrawn or hostile ones. The consistent finding is that relationships do better when coping is shared and supportive, and worse when it turns disengaged, protective, or adversarial.

article continues after advertisement

Supportive coping includes empathic responses, practical help, and active engagement, among others. More collaborative forms involve both partners treating stress as something they’re facing together, rather than something one person has to absorb alone. These patterns are linked to better relationship quality and better individual well-being.

Dignity protection is what this often looks like on the ground. It’s the partner who doesn’t join in when you’re being lightly mocked in a group setting. The one who corrects a mischaracterization about you instead of letting it sit for convenience. The one who always speaks about you with respect, even when you’re not in the room.

Hostility, disengagement, or emotional withdrawal during stress is associated with worse relational outcomes. They can fundamentally shape how partners see themselves. People who are repeatedly met with negativity or withdrawal under stress tend to report more negative self-evaluations over time.

That’s where dignity matters most. Because when someone consistently has your back in stressful or socially exposed moments, you’re shown, with both words and actions, that you matter, that you’re safe, and that your partner chooses your side over anyone else’s. That’s loyalty at its finest.

Neither of these two habits is especially dramatic. But that’s the point. Loyalty, in practice, shouldn’t have to be a bold declaration. It looks like someone consistent enough that you don’t have to second-guess and steady enough that you don’t feel alone when things get messy.
